title: UEFA Declares Loss of Confidence in FIFA President Infantino Over World Cup Sell-Off
excerpt: European soccer's governing body delivered its sharpest rebuke of Gianni Infantino after FIFA was forced to abandon a $4.2 billion plan to sell private stakes in the World Cup.
body:
• UEFA declared it has lost confidence in FIFA President Gianni Infantino after world soccer's governing body abandoned a controversial plan to sell a 20% stake in World Cup commercial rights to private investors.
  • The scheme, which aimed to raise up to $4.2 billion through a new subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise, was unanimously rejected by UEFA's 55 member associations and opposed by multiple confederations.
  • Senior Infantino adviser Carlos Cordeiro, the former U.S. Soccer president, resigned on Friday, saying he opposed the proposal "unequivocally."
  • Infantino faces re-election in March 2027, with growing questions about his political survival after the backlash.

UEFA Slams "Shabby" Deal After FIFA Retreat

European soccer's governing body UEFA declared on Saturday that it has lost confidence in FIFA President Gianni Infantino, delivering its most forceful public rebuke of world football's top official after he was forced to abandon a hugely controversial plan to sell private stakes in the World Cup.

In a blistering statement, UEFA welcomed FIFA's decision to withdraw the proposal but made clear the reversal had not repaired the damage.

"We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account."

— UEFA statement

FIFA and Infantino had announced plans on Tuesday to create FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a separate subsidiary that would sell approximately 20% of its equity to private investors in exchange for up to $4.2 billion. The unit would have controlled the commercial and operational rights to FIFA's marquee tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.

A Week of Escalation

The proposal triggered a swift and fierce backlash. UEFA's 55 member associations unanimously rejected the plan earlier in the week, with the confederation threatening to boycott FIFA competitions entirely. CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation followed suit, eroding any path to the majority vote from FIFA's 211 member associations that Infantino would have needed.

By Friday, the revolt had penetrated Infantino's inner circle. Carlos Cordeiro, the former U.S. Soccer president who served as a senior adviser to the FIFA chief, resigned from his position.

"I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup. Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally."

— Carlos Cordeiro, former senior adviser to Infantino

The major investor behind FFE was identified as Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, adding a politically charged dimension to the controversy.

Governance Crisis Deepens

UEFA's statement, while stopping short of an explicit call for Infantino's resignation, cast the episode as a fundamental governance failure. The confederation said Infantino had promised transparency when he first sought the FIFA presidency in 2016 but had delivered the opposite.

"The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent," UEFA said, adding that it would work with its associations and other confederations in the coming weeks to "devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again."

After backtracking, Infantino said his goal was now to "bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game."

What Comes Next

Infantino faces re-election in March 2027, and the swift collapse of the FFE proposal has raised open questions about whether he can survive politically. The Dutch football federation KNVB said it "no longer has confidence in his leadership," while the Belgian FA reaffirmed its commitment to "a strong, independent and sustainable model for international football."

UEFA called the withdrawal "a victory for the whole game" but warned: "The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun."

For fans and football officials worldwide, the episode has crystallized long-simmering concerns about FIFA's decision-making under Infantino, who has overseen an expansion of World Cup formats and controversial hosting decisions since taking office in 2016.
nri_angle: The governance crisis at FIFA may affect how major tournaments like the World Cup are commercialized and broadcast, relevant to millions of Indian soccer fans worldwide.
